The measuring resumes after the house has been described, and Gill has the prophet led into the surrounding court on the north side. Clarke reads the move differently, taking him into the priests' court, called outer only relative to the temple, with the people's court beyond. Ellicott keeps the plainer sense of outer and works out the building's extent: a hundred cubits long, and since a later passage shows it did not reach the western wall, it must have run the remaining length west of the separate place. Keil and Delitzsch call it a cell-building.

The dimensions are given from outside. Ellicott points out that a door on the north put the entrance necessarily in the outer court, that the long axis must run east and west, so the fifty-cubit width reached into the court as far as the inner gateways, and that the measurements are external because the prophet never went in. Wesley sets the house itself on their southern prospect.

The galleries are harder. Ellicott calls the phrase difficult in the original, where the word rendered against is literally unto the face of and the word for storeys is missing; his best sense is a gallery in the third storey of each block, set on the facing sides so the two buildings looked at each other. Wesley divides them otherwise, one gallery toward the inner court and another toward the pavement, the chambers between.

Then comes the crux of the chapter, a way of one cubit. Keil and Delitzsch demolish the reading that makes it the width of the entrances, on three grounds: the word is used collectively after one that is not, and before a plural for their doors; a way is not an entrance or a doorway; and an opening of a single cubit into a large building would bear no proportion to a walk of ten. No suitable meaning, they conclude, can be got from the words as they stand. Ellicott suspects the text instead. The Greek reads a hundred, and the change needs only a transposition of the first letters of one word and one letter altered in the other — precisely the transposition that occurs later in this chapter, where the Hebrew margin corrects it. A walk twenty inches wide could serve no purpose; one ten wide and a hundred long reaches exactly to the steps of the inner north gate, where the sacrifices were killed and dressed, so that the portions carried to these chambers went the shortest way. Wesley keeps the cubit and makes it a ledge along the building, called a way though nobody walked on it.

The three storeys are explained by the galleries. Gill has them one above another, the middle shorter than the lowest and the top shorter still; Wesley insists the word points to height, not length. Ellicott renders it that the upper chambers were shortened because the galleries ate into them, the gallery belonging only to the third storey. The remark that these had no pillars like the pillars of the courts tells him both that the galleries had no external support and that the courts had pillars, most likely cloisters as in the later temple.

A screen closes the description. Ellicott observes that the word for wall here is a different one, used elsewhere of a hedge and a vineyard fence, and that its fifty cubits make it a screen at the eastern end, keeping the outer court from seeing in while the priests changed their garments. Gill reads it as the grace that separates and protects. Henry takes the block morally: private rooms stand about the place of public worship because attending the ordinances excuses nobody from the closet, and within sight of the house because private devotion prepares for public rather than replacing it. The walk before them, he adds, is where those lodging there talked for mutual edification.

The second block repeats the first and is dispatched quickly, Gill noting only that chambers stood on the eastern side too. Ellicott renders it as a way in front of them like the northern chambers, matching in length, breadth, exits and doors, and warns that the next verse contains a word found nowhere else; the wall in it he identifies with the screen already described, so that the path from the gate porch met the passage beside the chambers at right angles. He closes with an admission worth having: unlike the rest of the vision, these chambers have no counterpart in the older building.

The use of the rooms follows. Ellicott takes both clauses to concern the priests' portion, and reasons that uncooked flesh cannot have been laid where the eating was done, the boiling happening elsewhere; the building was long enough to be divided into several rooms. He notices what is missing: no peace offerings, the law never having required those to be eaten in a holy place. Wesley makes some of the chambers a store-house for what was not in present use.

The garments are the other business of the place. Clarke states the rule flatly: the vestments were for ministry only, might not be worn in the outer court, and were left in these chambers when the service ended. Ellicott reaches it more cautiously, since the law nowhere states the rule in general terms but only implies it, so that he takes the prophet to be recognising an ancient custom rather than making a new one.

Then he is led out and the whole precinct measured, and the size becomes the question. Gill has him begin at the east, taking four equal sides in turn. Ellicott makes the arithmetic explicit: the rod was six cubits, so five hundred rods is three thousand cubits, near enough a mile — an enclosure as large as the walls of the old city ever held, and impossible on that hill. Attempts have been made to shrink it, but he holds the rod decisive, and quotes Keil that the later chapters on dividing the sanctuary from the land agree with this and prove the temple was never meant to stand in the old city — nor, he adds, anywhere on earth, the vision not being designed for material realisation. Keil and Delitzsch confirm that the extent has divided opinion since ancient times. Clarke says it is no wonder the place was called a city; Gill concludes no material building can be meant, since no such edifice ever stood.

The wall is read as the point of the measurement. Ellicott distinguishes it from the slight screen mentioned earlier, the word being that used of the massive outer wall, and gives its object as protecting the sanctity of the house. Clarke describes what it excluded: no stranger or unclean person might enter the consecrated ground, while the outer space admitted anyone. He cites the historian for a low barrier in his own day carrying notices in two languages that forbade foreigners to pass on pain of death. Henry draws the rule out of it: a difference is to be put between common and sacred things, and a distance between worldly and religious actions, so that we come to worship with a solemn pause.

The scale is finally read as promise, not architecture. Henry measures the sides at about an English mile and calls the whole the suburbs of a mystical temple, signifying how far the church would extend when all nations were discipled — fulfilled in part already, and to be finished when the fulness of the Gentiles comes in. Wesley repeats that reading almost word for word, though his circuit runs to eight miles and Henry's to four. Gill reaches the same place, taking the enormous square for the largeness of the church in the latter day.
